notes: Chapters 1–4 use Hebrew alphabetic patterns. Here each of the twenty-two verses begins with the next letter. English lineation preserves the poem's movement without claiming to reproduce that alphabetic form. Jerusalem speaks and is spoken about as a woman.

The poem uses impurity, skirts, and nakedness to describe the city's disgrace. The imagery is preserved as ancient lament language; it does not make sexual humiliation an approved response to wrongdoing.

The opening question of verse 12 is difficult and can also be read as an appeal to passersby. The verb for binding the yoke in verse 14 is rare; some readings understand watching over the rebellions instead. Fire and net images are not reduced to one literal event.
The closing request asks that enemies suffer as Jerusalem has suffered. The draft keeps this as the afflicted city's prayer, without adding a resolution or endorsement of retaliation.
vocabulary: Appointed assembly
The word also used for a feast or appointed meeting is turned here into a gathering that crushes the city's young men.
Forced labor
Compulsory service imposed on a subject population, reversing the city's former rank.

notes: Verse 6's shelter/garden comparison is difficult. Verse 11 keeps “liver,” an ancient bodily expression of intense distress. “My people” represents the personifying expression “daughter of my people,” not a separate daughter belonging to the speaker.
This chapter places the Hebrew letter pe before ayin. The text follows that order. Verse 18 shifts abruptly from “their hearts” to addressing Zion's wall and its eye; the personification is retained.
The city's appeal names children eaten in famine, bodies in the streets, and killing attributed directly to God. Its protest remains explicit alongside the earlier account of wrongdoing.
vocabulary: Horn
An image of strength: Israel's horns are cut off, while the enemies' horn is raised.
Watch
A division of the night for keeping guard. The appeal is to cry out repeatedly through the night.

notes: Each Hebrew letter begins three successive verses in this sixty-six-verse poem. The opening speaker is a man, but the poem does not name him. The source uses “he,” not repeated instances of the divine name, until verse 18.

The word rendered “endurance” can also mean lasting strength or splendor. Verse 19 can be an appeal to remember or a statement of recollection. The pinned Hebrew of verse 22 says “we have not come to an end”; the familiar “his love never ceases” follows a different construal or reading.

These reflections remain inside the afflicted speaker's poem. “God” in verse 28 clarifies an implied agent; another reading takes the burden as something the man assumes. “From his heart” in verse 33 concerns willingness or desire. Verse 36 can ask whether the Lord sees, or state that he does not approve. Verse 39 literally speaks of a man's sins, with their consequences understood here.
The poem returns from hope to “you have not forgiven” and blocked prayer, then ends with a petition for vengeance. These turns have not been smoothed into a single reassuring conclusion.

Verse 51's relation to the city's daughters is uncertain; it may mean grief because of them or more than theirs. Verse 53 can describe stones thrown at the speaker or a stone placed over the pit. Verse 56's plea for relief can also refer to breathing or sighing. The “covering” of the heart in verse 65 is obscure and may imply hardness or obstruction.
vocabulary: Sons of his quiver
An image for arrows. “Kidneys” names the inner body struck by them.
Wormwood
A bitter plant used here as an image of suffering.
Portion
One's allotted share or inheritance. The speaker calls the LORD his portion.

sections.1: The man who has seen affliction

notes: The animal comparisons reflect the poem's ancient imagery. “Punishment” in verse 6 can also be “guilt”; the final hands clause may concern attack or help. “Consecrated ones” in verse 7 may mean Nazirites or nobles. The precise minerals represented by coral and sapphire are uncertain.
The mothers are called compassionate even as famine leads to cannibalism. The next movement specifically names bloodshed by prophets and priests. Neither feature has been removed.

“The LORD's anointed” refers in this setting to the captured king. The promise to Zion and warning to Edom are retained alongside the book's later unresolved ending. This chapter, like chapters 2 and 3, places pe before ayin in its alphabetic order.
vocabulary: Cup
The allotted experience of judgment, pictured as intoxicating drink.
Scarlet
Costly colored clothing or cloth, marking the comfort in which these people were raised.

sections.17: The help that did not come

notes: This communal prayer has twenty-two verses, matching the Hebrew alphabet's length, but its verses are not alphabetically arranged.

Verse 5 compresses pursuit and the neck image. Giving the hand in verse 6 signifies submission. Verse 7's inherited burden stands beside the confession in verse 16. The hanging in verse 12 may be by the victims' hands or at the enemies' hands. Verse 13 may refer to carrying millstones or being put to grinding labor.
The verb in this setting describes sexual violation. “Raped” makes the harm explicit; “virgins” preserves the group specifically named in the second line.

The last verse can be read “unless you have utterly rejected us” or as a stronger assertion, “For you have utterly rejected us.” Either way, the book ends with rejection and anger still in question. No reassuring answer has been added.
vocabulary: City gate
A place of gathering, public discussion, and judgment; its silence marks the loss of ordinary civic life.
